1.q: וַ⁠תְּהִ֤י הַ⁠מִּלְחָמָה֙ אֲרֻכָּ֔ה בֵּ֚ין בֵּ֣ית שָׁא֔וּל וּ⁠בֵ֖ין בֵּ֣ית דָּוִ֑ד
1.note: The author is using this clause to describe something that was ongoing. This provides the background for other events he will describe that began to happen during this time. Connect this clause to the story in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [For a long time after that there was war between the house of Saul and between the house of David.]

1.q: וַ⁠תְּהִ֤י הַ⁠מִּלְחָמָה֙ אֲרֻכָּ֔ה בֵּ֚ין בֵּ֣ית שָׁא֔וּל וּ⁠בֵ֖ין בֵּ֣ית דָּוִ֑ד
1.note: In this context, the term **house** refers to the family line of a king, which might include several descendants who were his successors as king. Your language may use this term in the same way, or it may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language, as the UST does. Alternate translation: [the royal house of Saul … the royal house of David] or [the dynasty of Saul … the dynasty of David]

1.q: וְ⁠דָוִד֙ הֹלֵ֣ךְ וְ⁠חָזֵ֔ק וּ⁠בֵ֥ית שָׁא֖וּל הֹלְכִ֥ים וְ⁠דַלִּֽים
1.note: The phrases **going and strong** and **going and weak** express single ideas. The word **going** indicates that the strength and weakness grew greater over time. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express these meanings in a different way. Alternate translation: [And David kept getting stronger, but the house of Saul kept getting weaker]

1.q: וְ⁠דָוִד֙ הֹלֵ֣ךְ וְ⁠חָזֵ֔ק וּ⁠בֵ֥ית שָׁא֖וּל הֹלְכִ֥ים וְ⁠דַלִּֽים
1.note: The author is using **David** to represent David and all those who supported him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And David and his supporters kept getting stronger]

2.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens later in the story. Three of these sons, **Amnon**, Absalom, and Adonijah, will figure prominently in the narrative. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Now David’s wives bore him sons]
Your language may have its own term or expression for this relationship. Alternate translation: [And his eldest]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [who was born to Ahinoam the Jezreelitess] or [whose mother was Ahinoam the Jezreelitess]

3.note: The author is using the adjectives **second** and **third** as nouns to mean certain people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases, here and in verses 4 and 5. Alternate translation: [And his second son … And his third son]

Your language may have its own way of showing that someone or something is first, second, third, or fourth in a series. If so, you can use it here and in verses 4 and 5. Alternate translation: [And son number two … And son number three] or [And his next son … And his next son]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:2. Alternate translation: [the widow of]

5.note: The author expects his readers to understand that this phrase applies to all of the women he lists here, not just to **Eglah**. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. (The author explains in 5:13 that David had concubines in addition to wives. These sons of his wives had rights of inheritance, and so they competed to succeed David as king, as much of the later story relates.) Alternate translation: [All of these women were David’s wives]

The expression **were born** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [David’s wives bore them to him] or [They bore them to him]

Since this statement duplicates information that is already in verse 2, it might seem like extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you might leave it out. However, see the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of how this statement provides a summary conclusion to the list and of how you might present the whole list in a way that is natural in your language and culture.

6.note: The author is using the word translated **And it happened** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event. Alternate translation: [During this time] or [Meanwhile]
See how you translated these expressions in [3:1](ta:03).

7.note: Here the author is introducing Rizpah as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Saul had a concubine named Rizpah who was the daughter of Aiah]
The pronoun **he** refers to Ishbosheth. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then Ishbosheth said to Abner]

Ishbosheth is using the question form to rebuke Abner. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not have gone in to the concubine of my father!]

Ishbosheth is referring to sexual relations in a polite way by using the phrase **gone in to**. Depending on what is appropriate in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [slept with]

8.note: The author is describing Abner becoming extremely angry by association with the way a person’s skin may become hot when he is angry. Your culture may also associate anger with heat, and if so, you could use its characteristic expression in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [And Abner became steaming mad] or [And Abner became extremely angry]

The author is using the term **words** to represent what Ishbosheth said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Ishbosheth had said to him]

Abner is using one part of a dog, his **head**, to mean an entire dog. He may be doing this to make his statement more elaborate and emphatic. Your language may have its own way of doing this. Alternate translation: [Am I some kind of dog that is to Judah]

Abner is using the question form to express anger and deny that he is worthless. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for those purposes, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I am not the head of a dog that is to Judah!] or [I am not some kind of dog that is to Judah!]

In this culture, people considered wild dogs dirty and regarded them with contempt. Abner is suggesting that the Judeans are contemptible for not supporting Saul’s son as their next king. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I am not some contemptible Judean!]

8.q: הַ⁠יּ֨וֹם אֶֽעֱשֶׂה־חֶ֜סֶד עִם־בֵּ֣ית ׀ שָׁא֣וּל אָבִ֗י⁠ךָ אֶל־אֶחָי⁠ו֙ וְ⁠אֶל־מֵ֣רֵעֵ֔⁠הוּ
8.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **kindness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I am treating your father Saul’s descendants, brothers, and friends kindly] or [I am remaining loyal to the house of Saul your father, to his brothers, and to his friends]

Here, **hand** represents the capability of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I have not delivered you into David’s power] or [and I have not allowed David to overpower you]

Abner is using this possessive form to mean iniquity committed against a woman. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [you charge me with committing iniquity against a woman]
See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of how, if Abner had actually had sexual relations with Rizpah, that would have been a symbolic action asserting a claim to be the king.

9.note: Abner swears in this verse that he is going to do something, but he does not describe until the next verse what he is going to do. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could create a verse bridge for verses 9–10 and have Abner first describe what he is going to do and then swear that he will do it. (That would not change the meaning, only the order of the information.) The UST models one way to do that.

9.q: כֹּֽה־יַעֲשֶׂ֤ה אֱלֹהִים֙ לְ⁠אַבְנֵ֔ר וְ⁠כֹ֖ה יֹסִ֣יף ל֑⁠וֹ כִּ֗י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר נִשְׁבַּ֤ע יְהוָה֙ לְ⁠דָוִ֔ד כִּֽי־כֵ֖ן אֶֽעֱשֶׂה־לּֽ⁠וֹ
9.note: Following the custom of his culture, Abner is using a conditional statement to swear an oath. What he states as a condition (“if”) is what he is swearing to do. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put the condition before the consequence. Alternate translation: [I swear that I will do for David according to what Yahweh has sworn to him, and if I do not, then may God do thus to Abner, and thus may he add to him]

9.q: כֹּֽה־יַעֲשֶׂ֤ה אֱלֹהִים֙ לְ⁠אַבְנֵ֔ר וְ⁠כֹ֖ה יֹסִ֣יף ל֑⁠וֹ כִּ֗י כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֨ר נִשְׁבַּ֤ע יְהוָה֙ לְ⁠דָוִ֔ד כִּֽי־כֵ֖ן אֶֽעֱשֶׂה־לּֽ⁠וֹ
9.note: Because he is swearing an oath, Abner is speaking about himself solemnly in the third person. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [Thus may God do to me, Abner, and thus may he add to me]

9.q: כֹּֽה־יַעֲשֶׂ֤ה אֱלֹהִים֙ לְ⁠אַבְנֵ֔ר וְ⁠כֹ֖ה יֹסִ֣יף ל֑⁠וֹ
9.note: When Abner says **thus may he add**, he is using a common expression of his culture. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Thus may God do to Abner, and may he do even worse]

9.q: כֹּֽה־יַעֲשֶׂ֤ה אֱלֹהִים֙ לְ⁠אַבְנֵ֔ר וְ⁠כֹ֖ה יֹסִ֣יף ל֑⁠וֹ
9.note: The word **Thus**: (1) could refer to what Abner describes in the next verse. Abner could be saying that if he does not take away the privileged position of Saul’s family, then he wants God to take away his privileged position as a powerful leader. The UST models one way to express that meaning. (2) could be a general expression introducing the entire statement as a reference to severe punishment. Alternate translation: [May God punish me, Abner, very severely]

10.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:12. Alternate translation: [to cause the kingdom to pass over from the descendants of Saul]

Abner is using the term **kingdom** to mean a king’s rule over the Israelites, not the Israelites themselves over whom he would rule. Alternate translation: [to cause the kingship to pass over from the descendants of Saul]

Here, Abner is speaking as if the **kingdom** might physically **pass over** from one location to another. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to cause the descendants of Saul no longer to rule as kings]

Abner is speaking as if he would physically **raise up** the **throne** of David to a high position above Israel and Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express his meaning using an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and to establish the rule of David]

Abner is referring to all of the Israelite territory by naming two extremes, **Dan** (a city in the far north) and **Beersheba** (a city in the far south). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [over the entire territory of Israel and Judah]

11.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Ishbosheth. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Ishbosheth was not able]

The author is using the term **word** to represent what Ishbosheth might have said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to say anything further]

12.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֖ר לְ⁠מִי־אָ֑רֶץ לֵ⁠אמֹ֗ר כָּרְתָ֤⁠ה בְרִֽיתְ⁠ךָ֙ אִתִּ֔⁠י
12.note: The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. Alternate translation: [saying, “To whom {is} the land? Cut your covenant with me]

Abner is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Abner could mean: (1) that he, not Ishbosheth, actually controls the **land**, so if David makes a covenant **with** him, he can deliver **all of Israel** to David. Alternate translation: [The land is under my control!]; (2) that since Yahweh promised David the kingship, Abner will help him become the king of all of Israel on that basis. Alternate translation: [You are the rightful king of the land!]

Abner is using **Cut your covenant** as a common expression of his culture to mean “make your covenant.” If this phrase would not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Make a covenant with me]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:12.

Abner is using his **hand** to represent himself in the act of accompanying and assisting David. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will be with you]

In telling David he will be **with** him, Abner is using a common expression of his culture to mean that he will help him. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will support you]

Here, Abner is speaking as if he would physically make the Israelites **turn** in a different direction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to make all the Israelites accept you as their king]

13.note: The pronoun **he** refers to David. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Then David said]

David is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will cut** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is making a commitment to Abner. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I agree to cut a covenant with you]

13.q: אַ֣ךְ דָּבָ֣ר אֶחָ֡ד אָנֹכִי֩ שֹׁאֵ֨ל מֵ⁠אִתְּ⁠ךָ֤ לֵ⁠אמֹר֙ לֹא־תִרְאֶ֣ה אֶת־פָּנַ֔⁠י כִּ֣י ׀ אִם־לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י הֱבִיאֲ⁠ךָ֗ אֵ֚ת מִיכַ֣ל בַּת־שָׁא֔וּל בְּ⁠בֹאֲ⁠ךָ֖ לִ⁠רְא֥וֹת אֶת־פָּנָֽ⁠י
13.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Only one thing I am asking from you. You will not see my face unless you bring Michal, the daughter of Saul, to my face when you come to see my face.]

13.q: לֹא־תִרְאֶ֣ה אֶת־פָּנַ֔⁠י כִּ֣י ׀ אִם־לִ⁠פְנֵ֣י הֱבִיאֲ⁠ךָ֗ אֵ֚ת מִיכַ֣ל
13.note: If it would appear in your language that David was making a statement and then contradicting it, you could reword this as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [You will only see my face if you bring Michal]

Here, **face** represents personal presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You will not come into my presence … when you come into my presence]

David is using **face** to represent his whole person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [back to me]

15.note: Since David refers to Michal as “my wife” in the previous verse, it may not be appropriate in your language and culture to describe Paltiel as **{her} husband** here. If that is the case, you can use a different expression. Alternate translation: [the man to whom her father Saul had given her]

Here the author is introducing Paltiel as a new participant in the story. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [a man named Paltiel who was the son of Laish]

See the discussion in the Introduction to this chapter of why this man is called **Paltiel** here but Palti when he first appears in the story in 1 Samuel 25:44. We recommend that you use these two different versions of his name in these places in your translation.

16.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:15.

The phrase **going and weeping** expresses a single idea. The word **weeping** tells in what way Paltiel was **going**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [going tearfully]

Abner could be using the term **Go** to tell Paltiel: (1) that he must now **return**. **Bahurim** was near the border of Judah, and Abner did not want Paltiel to enter the territory that David was ruling. Alternate translation: [It is time for you to return]; (2) that Paltiel must leave that place, where Michal was, and return to his home without her. Alternate translation: [Leave here and return home]

17.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture. Alternate translation: [Meanwhile, Abner had been speaking with the elders of Israel]

The author is using the term **word** to represent what Abner said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now Abner had sent a message to the elders of Israel]

Abner is using **Both yesterday and the third day** as a common expression of his culture to mean the way things had been previously. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [In the past]

18.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:6.

18.q: עֲשׂ֑וּ כִּ֣י יְהוָ֗ה אָמַ֤ר אֶל־דָּוִד֙ לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר בְּ⁠יַ֣ד ׀ דָּוִ֣ד עַבְדִּ֗⁠י הוֹשִׁ֜יעַ אֶת־עַמִּ֤⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מִ⁠יַּ֣ד פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וּ⁠מִ⁠יַּ֖ד כָּל־אֹיְבֵי⁠הֶֽם
18.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [since Yahweh spoke about David, saying, ‘By the hand of David my servant, I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from the hand of all of their enemies,’ do it]

18.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֔ר בְּ⁠יַ֣ד ׀ דָּוִ֣ד עַבְדִּ֗⁠י הוֹשִׁ֜יעַ אֶת־עַמִּ֤⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מִ⁠יַּ֣ד פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וּ⁠מִ⁠יַּ֖ד כָּל־אֹיְבֵי⁠הֶֽם
18.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [saying that by the hand of David his servant he would save his people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from the hand of all of their enemies]

Here, **hand** represents the actions of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Through the actions of David my servant]

Here, **hand** represents the power or control of a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of the Philistines and from the power of all of their enemies] or [from the control of the Philistines and from the control of all of their enemies]

19.note: The author is using the term **ears** to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the hearing of Benjamin … in the hearing of David] or [to Benjamin in person … to David in person]

19.q: אֵ֤ת כָּל־אֲשֶׁר־טוֹב֙ בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וּ⁠בְ⁠עֵינֵ֖י כָּל־בֵּ֥ית בִּנְיָמִֽן
19.note: See the discussion of the phrase **good in the eyes of** in the Introduction to this chapter. Alternate translation: [everything that Israel and the house of Benjamin had decided was the right thing to do]
Here, **Israel** represents the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Israelites]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:12. Alternate translation: [the whole tribe of Benjamin]

20.note: Bringing a round and significant number of men with him was a symbolic action by which Abner showed respect for David. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action. Alternate translation: [and he brought 20 men with him to show respect for David]

21.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 2:14. Alternate translation: [Let me take action]

Even though Abner is addressing David directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **my lord the king** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [to you, my lord the king]

Abner says **all of Israel** as an generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [leaders from throughout Israel]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:12. Alternate translation: [so they may make a covenant with you]

Abner is using David’s **soul** to represent all of him as a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you desire]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [peacefully]

22.note: The author is using this possessive form to mean not people who served both David and Joab but people who served David, including Joab. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Joab and other servants of David]

22.q: וְ⁠אַבְנֵ֗ר אֵינֶ֤⁠נּוּ עִם־דָּוִד֙ בְּ⁠חֶבְר֔וֹן כִּ֥י שִׁלְּח֖⁠וֹ וַ⁠יֵּ֥לֶךְ בְּ⁠שָׁלֽוֹם
22.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [But since David had sent Abner away and he had gone in peace, he was not with David in Hebron]

23.note: Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and Joab was told]

24.note: Joab is using the question form to challenge David for letting Abner go. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You have done something that you should not have done!]

Joab is using the question form to express his strong disapproval of David letting Abner go. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There was no good reason to send him away, so that going, he has gone!]

Joab is repeating forms of the verb “go” in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [and he has completely gone]

25.note: Joab is speaking of the first and last actions of a military campaign, **going out** and **coming in**, in order to mean military activities as a whole. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the same expression in 1 Samuel 29:6. Alternate translation: [and to find out about how you conduct your military campaigns]

Joab speaks in the present tense to David of things **you are doing** in order to describe actions that David has not yet done but that Joab believes he is planning to do. Use the verb form in your language that is natural for referring to planned future actions. Alternate translation: [and to find out everything that you are planning to do]

27.note: The author assumes that his readers will know that by **the middle of the gate**, he is referring to an area within the city wall between the openings that led out of the city and into the city. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. The UST models one way to do that.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **quiet**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [quietly]

27.q: וַ⁠יַּכֵּ֤⁠הוּ שָׁם֙ הַ⁠חֹ֔מֶשׁ וַ⁠יָּ֕מָת בְּ⁠דַ֖ם עֲשָׂה־אֵ֥ל אָחִֽי⁠ו
27.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about why Joab killed Abner before the information about how he did it. Alternate translation: [And for the blood of Asahel his brother, he struck him there in the stomach, and he died]

27.q: וַ⁠יַּכֵּ֤⁠הוּ שָׁם֙ הַ⁠חֹ֔מֶשׁ וַ⁠יָּ֕מָת בְּ⁠דַ֖ם עֲשָׂה־אֵ֥ל אָחִֽי⁠ו
27.note: The pronoun **he** refers to Joab, while the pronoun **him** refers to Abner. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And for the blood of Asahel his brother, Joab struck Abner there in the stomach, and Abner died]

Here, **blood** represents the killing of Asahel for which Joab wanted to take revenge. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to avenge the death of Asahel his brother]

28.note: The implication is that David is referring not just to his current reign but to the continuing rule of his descendants. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and my royal dynasty]

Here, **blood** represents the killing of Abner. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [regarding the death of Abner]

The word **blood** is plural here because it refers to blood shed by violence. Your language may use the plural form of its word for blood to mean the same thing. If not, you could express the meaning in another way. Alternate translation: [of the bloodshed against Abner]

29.q: יָחֻ֨לוּ֙ עַל־רֹ֣אשׁ יוֹאָ֔ב וְ⁠אֶ֖ל כָּל־בֵּ֣ית אָבִ֑י⁠ו
29.note: The word as **it** refers back to “the blood of Abner” in the previous verse. If you translated “blood” with a plural form there, it may be natural for you to use a plural pronoun here. You could also state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Abner’s blood writhe on the head of Joab and to all of the house of his father]

29.q: יָחֻ֨לוּ֙ עַל־רֹ֣אשׁ יוֹאָ֔ב וְ⁠אֶ֖ל כָּל־בֵּ֣ית אָבִ֑י⁠ו
29.note: David is using the same common expression here that he used in 1:16, about blood being on someone’s **head**, to mean that a person was morally and legally responsible for something and would be punished for it. Here he uses a more vivid form of the expression and wishes that the blood of Abner would **writhe** on Joab’s head. This represents the sufferings of Joab and his extended family that David describes in the rest of the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May Joab and all of the house of his father painfully bear the responsibility for it]

The expression **the house of his father** refers to Joab’s extended family and descendants. Your language may have its own term or expression for such a group of related people. Alternate translation: [his extended family]

The expression **be cut off** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and may not be missing from the house of Joab] or [may there always be in the house of Joab]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:12. Alternate translation: [among the descendants of Joab]

The expression **stricken with leprosy** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [or a leper]

This expression could describe: (1) a person who, because of injury or illness, needs to use a staff to support himself when standing or walking. Alternate translation: [or a lame person]; (2) a man who, because of injury or weakness, cannot do strenuous work or fight in battles and so must do domestic work such as using a distaff (spindle) to wind wool into thread. Alternate translation: [or a weak man]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:12. Alternate translation: [or one dying in battle]

David is using the adjective **destitute** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [or someone who lacks bread]

David is using **bread** to represent all food or basic necessities. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [or someone who lacks food] or [someone who is desperately poor]

30.q: וְ⁠יוֹאָב֙ וַ⁠אֲבִישַׁ֣י אָחִ֔י⁠ו הָרְג֖וּ לְ⁠אַבְנֵ֑ר עַל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵמִ֜ית אֶת־עֲשָׂהאֵ֧ל אֲחִי⁠הֶ֛ם בְּ⁠גִבְע֖וֹן בַּ⁠מִּלְחָמָֽה
30.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand why David so greatly disapproved of what Joab had done. The author is contrasting the way Abner **killed** Asahel in battle (as he described in 2:23) with the way Joab and Abishai **murdered** Abner treacherously under peaceful conditions. If your language has different words for killing and murdering, it would be appropriate to use them here in your translation to show this contrast.

31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:4. Alternate translation: [the soldiers]

Tearing one’s **clothes** and wearing **sackcloth** were symbolic actions that showed intense grief and mourning in ancient Israelite culture. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of these actions in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [show your grief by tearing your clothes and wearing rough cloth]

Here David speaks of **Abner** to mean Abner’s body. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and walk in procession as mourners ahead of Abner’s body]

Here, **walking behind the bier** was a symbolic action by which David showed public respect for Abner and demonstrated that he had not been responsible for Abner’s death. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [King David himself followed the funeral procession to show his respect]

A **bier** is a kind of platform or frame used to carry a dead body to burial. If your readers would not be familiar with what a bier is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the stretcher carrying Abner’s body]

32.note: Here, the author is speaking as if **voice** were an object that could be lifted up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the king raised the volume of his voice and wept]

The phrase **lifted up his voice and wept** expresses a single idea. The words **lifted up his voice** describe in what way David **wept**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [And the king wept loudly]

33.note: David is using the question form to emphasize how wrong it was for Abner to have died the way he did. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Abner should not have died like the death of a fool!]

The implication is that Abner died in an unjust and dishonorable way, as if he were a criminal deserving death, when in fact he was not. You could indicate this if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Abner should not have been executed as if he had been a wicked person!]

34.q: יָדֶ֣⁠ךָ לֹֽא־אֲסֻר֗וֹת וְ⁠רַגְלֶ֨י⁠ךָ֙ לֹא־לִ⁠נְחֻשְׁתַּ֣יִם הֻגָּ֔שׁוּ כִּ⁠נְפ֛וֹל לִ⁠פְנֵ֥י בְנֵֽי־עַוְלָ֖ה נָפָ֑לְתָּ
34.note: David is speaking to Abner, who is dead and cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about how Abner was treacherously murdered. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Abner. Alternate translation: [His hands were not bound, and his feet were not put in shackles. He died like someone murdered by wicked men]

Here, bound **hands** and shackled **feet** represent being held as a prisoner. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You were not being held as a prisoner because you had been convicted of a crime]
See how you translated the expression similar to **falling** and **fallen** in 1:12. Alternate translation: [As dying to the face of sons of wickedness, you have died]

See how you translated the expression similar to **to the face of** in 2:17. Alternate translation: [As dying at the hands of sons of wickedness, you have died] or [You died because sons of wickedness killed you]
See how you translated the similar expression in 2:7. Alternate translation: [wicked men]
This could mean: (1) Alternate translation: [wept for him even more]; (2) Alternate translation: [wept for him again]

35.q: וַ⁠יָּבֹ֣א כָל־הָ⁠עָ֗ם לְ⁠הַבְר֧וֹת אֶת־דָּוִ֛ד לֶ֖חֶם בְּ⁠ע֣וֹד הַ⁠יּ֑וֹם
35.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about when this happened before the information about the people coming to David. Alternate translation: [Then, while it was still day, all of the people came to make David eat bread]

The author says **all of the people** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [Then the others in attendance came with concern]

The author is using **bread** to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [food] or [a meal]

35.q: כֹּ֣ה יַעֲשֶׂה־לִּ֤⁠י אֱלֹהִים֙ וְ⁠כֹ֣ה יֹסִ֔יף כִּ֣י אִם־לִ⁠פְנֵ֧י בֽוֹא־הַ⁠שֶּׁ֛מֶשׁ אֶטְעַם־לֶ֖חֶם א֥וֹ כָל־מְאֽוּמָה
35.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:9. Alternate translation: [If I taste bread or any of a thing to the face of the coming in of the sun, then may God do thus to me, and thus may he add]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:9. Alternate translation: [Thus may God do to me, and may he do even worse]

The word **Thus**: (1) could refer to the way Abner died a violent death. Alternate translation: [May God make me suffer a violent death, as Abner did, and even worse]; (2) could be a general expression introducing the entire statement as a reference to severe punishment. Alternate translation: [May God punish me very severely]

David not eating bread or anything else until sunset, not even a small taste, was a symbolic action that showed deep mourning and grief in ancient Israelite culture. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [if I fail to show proper morning by even tasting any food before sunset]
Here, **face** represents “before.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before the coming in of the sun]

David is using **the coming in of the sun** as a common expression of his culture to mean “sunset.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before the sun goes down] or [before sunset]

36.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:35. Alternate translation: [And the others in attendance noticed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:19. Alternate translation: [and they felt that he had done the right thing]

36.q: כְּ⁠כֹל֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר עָשָׂ֣ה הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֥י כָל־הָ⁠עָ֖ם טֽוֹב
36.note: The author says **everything that the king did was good in the eyes of all of the people** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [just as the people of Judah generally felt that David, their king, was doing the right things]

38.q: הֲ⁠ל֣וֹא תֵדְע֔וּ כִּי־שַׂ֣ר וְ⁠גָד֗וֹל נָפַ֛ל הַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה בְּ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
38.note: David is using the question form for emphasis when he makes a strong statement that his people should recognize Abner’s importance. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You must appreciate that a commander and great has fallen this day in Israel!]
See how you translated the similar expression in [3:1](ta:03). Alternate translation: [a great commander]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:12. Alternate translation: [has died]
David is using the term **this day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at this time]

39.note: The expression **anointed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [even though Yahweh has anointed me to be the king]
